Part of the fleet-wide OpenCode 2 migration tracked at https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/issues/374 (origin issue for the whole set).

Upstream migration guide: https://dev.opencode.ai/v2/docs/migrate-v1/

Two workstreams in this repo:

## 1. Config validation — `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` against OpenCode v2

- Load the repo config with OpenCode v2 (`@opencode/cli@2.1.4`) and record what it accepts and rejects.
- Config files, agents, commands, and skills under `.opencode/` are intended to be compatible; some v1 fields are **accepted but ignored** by v2. Hard rejections get fixed (PR); accepted-but-ignored fields get listed here so we can decide whether to keep them while runtimes are still migrating or drop them.
- Note: `.opencode/cli.json` already targets the v2 CLI schema (`https://opencode.ai/v2/cli.json`), while `.opencode/tui.jsonc` still exists alongside it (v2 auto-migrates tui.json → cli.json).

## 2. Plugin ports — v1 plugin API → v2 plugin API

v1 plugins do not run in v2 (new plugin API). Ours, in order of how much we depend on them:

- **mcpx bridge + mcpx-session** — `.opencode/plugin/mcpx-session.ts` is the plugin entry (imports `tool` and `Plugin` from `@opencode-ai/plugin`; default export is `async ({ directory, worktree, project, client }, options) => …`), backed by the `.opencode/plugin/mcpx/` modules (daemon client, ops). Backlog. Findings: `pkgs/mcpx/docs/opencode-plugin.md` §2 and §4.

**v1 plugins do not load in opencode v2** — no shim, no fallback (`packages/core/src/plugin/module.ts:60-73`). v2 needs a rewrite against `{id, setup}`, not a port.

What changes, each better than the v1 equivalent:

| v1 today | v2 |
| --- | --- |
| `shell.env` per command (carries sessionID) | `shell.create.before` has **no sessionID** → use `PUT /api/experimental/session/:id/environment` once per session |
| `experimental.chat.system.transform` | `session.hook("context")` → `event.system` (or a budgeted catalog in `event.tools`, diffed between turns) |
| `tool` map, un-namespaced | `tool.transform(e => e.add(...))` with a namespace |
| `tool.execute.after` sees success only | union on `status` — record failures too |

## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: find where OpenCode-native scheduled tasks can replace the Muse cron jobs that currently launch OpenCode — to save Muse tokens or raise throughput — with proper management and monitoring of those tasks and their outcomes. Study: ~/workspace/research_notes/opencode-scheduled-tasks-20261029/findings.md.

## Verdict: PARTIAL — the trigger exists, in OpenChamber, not OpenCode

- **OpenCode core has no scheduler.** Zero cron/timer code in packages/core|server|cli; sessions are purely event-driven.
- **OpenChamber has a real scheduled-tasks subsystem** (packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/): cron/daily/weekly/once with timezones, per-project + chats scopes, new-session-per-run (model/agent pinning, permission auto-accept, goal mode with token budget, sessions stamped metadata.kind='scheduled') or prompt-into-existing-session, cross-instance occurrence claiming, loop files (.agents/loops/*.md), REST + UI + CLI + an agent tool (openchamber_schedule).
- But it is a **prompt scheduler, not a job system**: state holds only the last run, no token capture, no alerting, in-code defaults of 4 global / 2 per-project concurrent runs, and a 30-minute run cap (vs ~90-minute shift windows).

## Migration waves (Claude input tokens, trailing-24h, runtime-DB attribution)

**Wave 1 (~3.4B/day of the fleet's ~5.1B/day):**
1. **Repo-queue worker shifts — ~2.26B/day, save ~2.1–2.2B.** The Muse layer is claim/checkpoint/terminal-verbs via repo-queue.py plus implem

## Symptom

Task 20708 (#3321 remainder, opencode lane, PR #12771 open, handed_off) is the only
candidate in every OpenCode claimant fire since the 2026-11-23 repair, and is never
launched:

- `repo-queue claim --handoff --platform openchamber` exits 5 ("no claimable task"),
  so claimant.py records `sink_claim_failed` / `cli_nonzero` each fire.
- `repo-queue claim --task 20708 --worker opencode-claimant` also exits 5.

## Cause

Lane ledger 10614 has `platform_limit = muse` with a recorded reason. In
`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue/src/turso_queue/lifecycle.rs` `platform_limit_refusal`,
a valid limit refuses every family except its own, and refuses a claim that declares
no family. The ledger note says "the designated OpenCode claimant can still take the
row by id (platform is a mark for by-id claims)", but the code does not honour that:
the only claim that passes is one declaring `--platform muse`, which would misstate
the claimant's family.

Net effect: the opencode-lane designation (the reason the limit was set to muse) and
the claimant's family cannot both be satisfied, so the row is unreachable by the
opencode claimant.

## Ask

Decide the intended contract and make the code and ledger agree:
1. Should an opencode-lane handoff with a `muse` limit be claimable by the opencode

   sanctioned family/by-id exception.
2. Or clear the limit (or set it to `opencode`) so the opencode claimant can

# Design mill: one fleet surface for OpenCode, OpenChamber, ID, and mcpx

Drew's design, dictated 2026-11-14. Protected design — do not close or drop without Drew.

## The idea in plain words

All automation and agent calls to OpenChamber, OpenCode, the ID binary, and the mcpx binary should go through subcommands of the fleet binary. At first this is mostly pass-through to the same underlying binary/endpoint, but fleet automatically resolves WHERE to talk: the right port on localhost, the right socket, the right endpoint path for that service on that host. Credentials are populated automatically and the caller can skip those fields. A raw mode (explicit endpoint path, raw POST body, explicit flag) always exists as an override.

This is a design mill with multiple passes, not one build. Passes are filed as sibling issues and cross-linked here.

## Cross-cutting rules Drew set

- Auto-resolution is the default; a specific flag overrides it. Defaults: the service's standard port on localhost or its socket.
- Endpoints can be customized per subprogram: a service may have a standard port, a website port, a homepage path, or a unique-ID custom path taken from settings, used raw.
- Everything exposed as a command should also be exposable as MCP and as REST (flag-gated, not all on at once). Later possibly GraphQL by the same switch.
- ID is the identity/transport layer of the whole system: many fleet commands will read/write the local or configured ID store, which may itself be remot

The Antigravity CLI (`agy` 1.5.9) ships a native ACP server (`agy acp`). Driven directly over stdio it completes a full round-trip with no auth ceremony (it uses the CLI's existing Google login; quota read tonight: weekly 0% used, resets 2026-11-30):

OpenClaw's acpx backend registers `agy` with command `/run/current-system/sw/bin/agy_acp_server` — Google's **standalone** agy-acp-server **1.2.1** (vendored as `pkgs/antigravity-acp`), a separate product from the CLI with **separate auth state** in `~/.gemini/antigravity-acp/` — a directory that does not exist: it has never been authenticated. Parent: #9093 (backup mesh) · Program: #8983 · Design: `doc/2026-11-23T16-34-18Z_design_backup_mesh/note.md` (landed with the #9093 design PR).
House rules: any schedule this creates lands its `doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md` row in the same PR; secrets by name only (Bitwarden at runtime, repo-archive pattern); builds/tests run via remote dispatch, never on the laptop or sandbox.

## Scope
The OpenCode session database joins the mesh. It is large on purpose (21.37 GB measured 2026-11-12, ~5.1 GB zstd) and has no scheduled off-laptop backup today (#10297, closed as the research tracker). Storage price is not the constraint; churn rate, restore time, and upload bandwidth are.

## Gate
This leg is **gated on research #9094** (OpenCode DB backup economics: measured churn, per-table growth model, costed comparison of full copy / zstd copy / restic deltas). Do not implement a scheme before #9094's comparison lands; the scheme choice is #9094's deliverable. When #9094 closes, this issue proceeds with the chosen scheme unmodified.

## Terms (from the design, whichever scheme #9094 picks)
- Targets: Google Drive + the laptop archive location (per the proto design §B); R2 joins only if #9094's costing says so.
- The DB is laptop-local state: it does NOT take a Turso home (size + churn break the appropriateness line, design §6).

## Acceptance
- [ ] #9094 closed with the scheme recorded; the chosen scheme implemented on a schedule.
- [ ] One full backup cycle completes; size/time record

## 1. OpenCode: "did not list any models yet" — root cause found, fork issue filed

T3 discovers models through the OpenCode server API. Live evidence from a T3-spawned server (fork 2.0.30): `GET /api/provider` returns all 13 providers with **0 models each**, while `GET /api/config` carries the full catalog that `bin/sync-models.mjs` maintains. So the data exists; the provider resource does not surface it.

→ Defect filed in the fork: developing-today/opencode#560 (merge resolved models into `/api/provider` + server test).

# Home-resolution contract: disposition the `os.homedir()` surface against #5762

Follow-up from the Phase 4 closing inventory audit (issue #5763, design issue #5762, contract in `files/designs/code-home-resolution-contract.md`, goal workspace keep-the-four-repos-healthy).

## Why this is filed separately

The Phase 4 audit (#5763) fixed the same-shape sites in-phase (invented substitute directories: root anchoring, CWD fallback, literal `~`, hardcoded `/home/user`). The `os.homedir()` surface is a genuinely different shape:

- Node's `os.homedir()` on POSIX returns `$HOME` when set, and otherwise the **passwd entry** for the process uid. It never invents a path — but passwd resolution is exactly the fallback the #5762 contract **declined as the default** ("another silent substitution"), so these sites do not conform either.
- The sites are concentrated in a different deploy unit (pm-stack aggregator/dispatch/exporters — long-running operator services whose config modules resolve `homedir()` once at module load) plus the bin/ proxy family. Converting them is a per-unit helper + test sweep of its own, not an audit fix.

## Inventory (origin/main 7dc4aefa23, from the #5763 audit)

bin/: opencode-route-proxy.mjs:73,77,80 (config/runtime-config/db path defaults; env overrides exist), opencode-acp-adapter.mjs:148, proxy-relay.mjs:56 (after an XDG_STATE_HOME override), proxy-supervise.mjs:71,72,372,399, check-opencode-go-seating.mjs:73, record.mjs:61.
Plugin: .opencode/plugin/mcpx/
title: home-resolution contract: disposition the os.homedir() surface against #5762

But `log show` returned nothing for dirhelper, so this isn't proven.

Relocated from dezren39/nix#218 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #181

## Summary

opencode v2 wraps every MCP server in its own code mode unless the server is configured `codemode: false`, and this machine's v1 does the same because `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL` is set. So mcpx's `/mcp` ends up as a tool called from a program the model wrote for opencode's interpreter, and nothing in mcpx's docs says to opt out. v2 also appends `?codemode=false` to remote MCP URLs so servers that bundle code mode can expose raw tools; mcpx ignores it. opencode runs permission checks and plugin hooks per child call, shows live status, and cancels on abort. The plugin's `mcpx_exec` makes one blocking POST and ignores the abort signal (the session and field bugs are #189).

Found while writing the comparison register (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/compare/`) and checked against the code at `05c78b2`. Each row below links its register entry, which carries the value, effort, risk, the specification text and every source.

## Gap

Drew's ruling (2026-11-03): a quota ask must terminate at the OpenCode server — not at a standalone proxy, and not at a credential store the server never sees. The Meta leg now complies: the quota gatherer (`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts`) asks the standing fork server's `GET /api/credential` (127.0.0.1:13420) for the credential, with the direct `opencode.db` read kept only as a transport-failure fallback (the quota CLI's combined-source shape, #2490).

The **OpenDesign leg cannot comply today**, and this issue names why precisely:

1. The OpenChamber quota module's OpenDesign provider (`server/lib/quota/providers/opendesign.js` in the OpenChamber fork) does not read the OpenCode credential machinery at all. The usage API it answers from (`https://amr-api.open-design.ai/api/auth/get-session`, `.../v1/workspaces/:id/billing/coding-plan-usage`) accepts only that session cookie (`Cookie: better-auth.session_token=…` + `x-vela-workspace-id` header). Parent program: #8983 · Feeds workstream B (backup mesh) · Proto design §B.

- `/home/user/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` = **21,368,037,376 B (19.9 GiB)**, ~448 MB internal freelist; **net allocated growth Nov 2 → Nov 12 = 0 bytes** (two dated full copies beside the DB are byte-identical in size); it was ~26 GB in the past and was pruned/vacuumed down. ## Design: automatic context propagation — every fleet action carries its origin

Origin: Drew, 2026-11-14. The goal: any command, session, secret lookup,
queue action, or file transfer in the fleet can be traced back to what
launched it — **automatically**, with zero per-call effort from models.
"If models have to stop and think about this every time, it has failed."

### The context record (what travels with every call)

Captured once at the outermost point available, inherited by everything

- OpenCode session id + parent session id; the OpenChamber scheduled

- The triggering message id (internal message id of the exact message

## Problem

`pm-stack/opencode-claimant/poll.py` takes 43–100s wall with only ~2s CPU per run (measured 2026-11-23: 73.8s by the #13112 triage, 55–100s in the #13112 evidence, 74.2s / 43.5s in Lane OI's timed runs). The time is waits on sequential external reads: turso ledger SELECTs via the turso-exec helper, broker queue queries (claimed + handed_off per queue), and the OpenCode server session list over a 28k+ root-session store.

#13112 fixed the starvation symptom by raising claimant.py's gate timeout 30s -> 300s (PR #13134). That leaves the gate budget ~3x the observed worst case, but poll latency itself keeps growing with the session store, and every claimant fire pays it.

## Ask

Reduce poll.py's own end-to-end latency so the gate budget has durable margin:

- Parallelize the independent external reads (ledger bindings, per-queue claimed/handed_off rows, session list, active-id set) instead of running them strictly sequentially.
- Bound each external read with an explicit per-read timeout and a recorded slow-read note, so one slow backend degrades the poll visibly instead of silently eating the budget.
- Keep the output contract byte-compatible: claimant.py's cap counting delegates to poll.py's pinned functions (#6609), so the JSON shape and the pinned semantics (root = no parentID, activity = time.updated falling back to time.created, finished = time.idle or a top-level outcome) must not change.

## Acceptance

- poll.py timed over 10 runs on the laptop: p99 wall tim

# C3 — Health hooks: failure-triggered checks that troubleshoot and report

Component of the reporting-architecture program (starter epic #9568).
Source: Drew's directive, Reports chat, 2026-11-13 09:11 CST.
Statements: S1.3.

## Scope

Checks like **"PM stack reachable"** and **"OpenCode working"** stop being
interval polls and become **hook scripts that fire on failure-to-connect**:

- On a failed connect (from any caller: PM stack surfaces, lane launches,
  aggregator ticks), the hook fires immediately, runs a bounded
  troubleshoot sequence (reachability, service state, auth/credential
  health, recent changes), and **reports what occurred** — a note to the
  queues/PM-health category chat, escalating to Reports when it is an
  exception and to the main chat when Drew is blocked.
- The hook records the incident into the PM-stack event store so C6 can

# Design mill pass 1: fleet subcommands for OpenCode, OpenChamber, ID, mcpx — pass-through with automatic endpoint + credential resolution

Part of the fleet-surface design mill (Drew, 2026-11-14). Parent issue cross-links all passes.

## What to design

Fleet gains subcommand families for each of the four tools (working names: `fleet opencode`, `fleet openchamber`, `fleet id`, `fleet mcpx`). In this first pass they mostly pass through to the same binary or endpoint as today — the value is that fleet owns resolution:

- **Endpoint resolution**: fleet knows each service's standard local endpoint (port on localhost, or unix socket) and uses it by default. Resolution is automatic unless the caller passes an explicit override flag.
- **Credential population**: when the target needs credentials, fleet fills them in from its normal secret routes; callers may omit those fields entirely.
- **Raw mode**: a caller can pass an exact endpoint path and a raw body (e.g. a raw POST) — the escape hatch that works for basically every tool.
- **Per-subprogram endpoint customization**: a service may expose more than one endpoint (ID: the iroh endpoint is the only guaranteed one today; ID may also host a website on a different standard port). Settings can declare a standard path, a homepage, or a unique-ID custom path for a subprogram; fleet uses that path raw.

Relocated from dezren39/nix#110 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #176

## Summary

mcpx has no model and deliberately never had one: `docs/consumer.md` records that "a configured provider with an API key, was not built and should not be. It is the one that makes mcpx an agent." Everything model-shaped in mcpx today borrows the caller's model through MCP sampling.

Two facts have changed since that was written, and together they invert the conclusion:

1. **MCP deprecated Sampling in `2026-07-28.**` The spec changelog's Deprecated section, item 1 (SEP-2577) deprecates Roots, Sampling and Logging, and names the migration explicitly: *"integrate directly with LLM provider APIs instead of Sampling."* Sampling is not the long-term channel; the spec says so.
2. **Nothing in the opencode line will ever send mcpx a sampling request.** `docs/opencode-plugin.md` §2.6: neither v1 nor v2 declares the `sampling` capability. v1 comments it out with issue links; v2 declares `roots` + `elicitation` only. The primary consumer of mcpx cannot answer the channel mcpx's only model path depends on.

So the question this issue settles is not "should mcpx sample?" — it is "where does mcpx's AI layer get a model, what does it expose, and how does it stay from becoming a second agent harness?"

## Problem (five words: silent mode deletion shadows claimant)

The opencode claimant's mode file (`~/.local/state/opencode-claimant/mode` on the laptop) is an unguarded single point of failure: when the file is missing, the claimant silently defaults to shadow mode (discovery only, no launches) with no signal. This has now bitten twice:

- 2026-11-08: mode file missing, claimant never launched anything until set to `live` by hand.
- 2026-11-14: `fires.jsonl` shows reads flipping live -> shadow at 14:46Z; the file was deleted ~5.5h after working live fires (deleter unattributed from available logs). This blocked the #9106 summit dispatch (`mode_not_live`, task 15354) until restored under Drew's authorization.

## Acceptance

- Mode file deletion or unreadability produces a VISIBLE alert within one surfacing cycle (wire into the #10141 silent-failure surfacing, now live) instead of a silent shadow fallback.
- Claimant startup/heartbeat records the mode it read and where from, so a flip is attributable in the log after the fact.
- Consider making the mode part of managed config (repo/systemd state) rather than a bare file any process can delete.
- A missing file must never again present as 'summits just aren't launching' for hours.

Refs: #9106, #10141, #9103. Filed from the 2026-11-14 summit-pool investigation (Track B).
title: claimant mode file: guard the silent-deletion single point of failure

House rules: any schedule this creates lands its `doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md` row in the same PR; secrets by name only (Bitwarden at runtime, repo-archive pattern); builds/tests run via remote dispatch, never on the laptop or sandbox.

## Scope
Laptop-local databases that hold real state and are not already covered by an existing leg land in the mesh via a Turso backup home, per the design's appropriateness line (§6): a local DB qualifies when it is SQL-shaped, modest in size, and has no other off-laptop copy. Candidates to disposition by name at implementation time: the pm-aggregator's local stores not covered by dashboard-backup, local atlas working DBs not covered by atlas-backup, and any SQLite state under the fleet tools' state dirs. Explicitly NOT this leg: the OpenCode session DB (own leg, gated on research #9094) and anything already covered by repo-archive / laptop-state / dashboard / atlas backups (no double coverage).

## Terms (from the design)
- Each qualifying DB gets a Turso home (`laptop-backup-<name>`); a scheduled export/import replaces the home's contents wholesale, weekly, staggered with the D1 leg.
- The inventory is the deliverable's first half: every laptop-local DB found is listed as qualifying, already-covered (naming the covering leg), or excluded-with-reason. An unlisted DB is a finding, not a silent ski

Leg of epic #1149 (quota-plane Stage 2). Filed at Drew's direction, 2026-10-29: *"there was supposed to be a unification in the 3 quota read methods."* There wasn't — three independent quota readers exist today, they resolve credentials three different ways, and they disagree. This issue is the unification leg of #1149; it cross-links the legs it absorbs or depends on rather than replacing them.

## The three readers

1. **OpenChamber web server `/api/quota/*`** — resolves credentials through the running OpenCode server's `GET /api/credential` projection (openchamber `server/index.js:1647`; projection `server/lib/opencode/auth.js:91, 203-230`, active rows only).
2. **`openchamber quota` CLI** — server-first, with a direct credential-store fallback (`openCodeLocalCredentialSource`, reading `opencode.db` read-only). Built 2026-10-27 under #1251, which deliberately switches to the store ONLY on transport failure and stamps each row `credentialSource: server|local`.
3. **PM-stack aggregator gatherer** (`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts:10-19, 116-149`) — reads `opencode.db` **directly, by design**, because the server-API path is known to diverge (#1251), replicates the server's projection itself, and additionally ingests bespoke per-provider file exporters (Meta: `pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs`). Writes `quota-current.json` on a ~15-minute systemd tick.

## Divergence evidence (2026-10-29, same evening, same pools)

- **Antigravity:** the hub (reader 3)
title: unify(quota-plane): one quota read path — server endpoint, CLI, and aggregator gatherer must share the direct credential-store read

## Summary

Implement spill v2 phase 2 from the #5787 design (`doc/2026-11-08_design_id5787.md`, §3): read replicas for a spilled world with an explicit staleness contract.

## Scope

- Replica read service over the authoritative journal stream: every read response carries the journal position it was served at (the replica's replay watermark).
- Bounded service: a replica beyond the configured lag bound refuses with retryable `replica-behind` instead of serving silently old state.
- Read-your-writes / monotonic reads: a client presenting its last acknowledged position is served only at a watermark ≥ that position (bounded wait or redirect to holder/DO).
- Presence rules: replicas may serve and originate only explicitly ephemeral, TTL'd, unjournaled presence data; session traffic that mutates goes to the holder and the append gate, always; no replica acknowledgment before the gate's durable receipt.

## Trigger / gating

**Do not start until trigger T2 fires:** the first production spill, or read load on a spilled world measurably served stale / refused at the holder. Design: #5787. Depends on: #3805, and on F1's pool/replica join (the phase-1 follow-on filed with the #5787 design).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Watermark, staleness-bound, and read-your-writes behaviours covered by deterministic tests, including the design §7 "replica serves during failover" case.
- [ ] No code path lets a replica acknowledge a mutation or promote presence data to durable state.
title: id: spill v2 phase 2 — read replicas with position-watermark staleness contract (#5787)

Part of the Atlas family (#5755); follows #6788 (the per-query Durable Object search cache Worker, shipped with **indefinite retention — no TTL, no eviction — per Drew's explicit order for v1**).

Indefinite retention is the v1 contract, not an oversight. Before it becomes load-bearing at scale, the eviction policy needs a design pass. Nothing here is urgent; this issue exists so the questions are on the record rather than discovered later.

## Questions to settle

1. **Corpus invalidation.** The cache key pins the embedding space (model revision + vector table) and ceiling, so a re-embedding of the corpus (new model/table) naturally orphans old entries — they simply stop being keyed. But a re-ingest under the *same* space (chunk content changes, shards added/renamed) leaves stale results served forever. Is that acceptable for a personal-corpus search surface, or do we need a corpus-generation component in the key (e.g. a registry epoch the service reports), accepting that a generation bump cold-starts the whole cache?
2. **Growth bound.** Entries hold an embedding (~12 KB JSON) + result envelope (observed ~17 KB at k=3; larger at k=50). At personal query volumes this is small for a long time; still, is there a count/size ceiling after which LRU-by-`searched_at`/`hit_count` eviction (both already recorded per entry) should engage?
3. **Manual purge.** A gated purge route (per-key delete; maybe per-prefix) is cheap to add to the Worker — worth having from the start of any poli
title: Atlas search Worker cache: eviction & invalidation policy (follow-up to #6788)

## Summary

Implement spill v2 phase 3 from the #5787 design (`doc/2026-11-08_design_id5787.md`, §4): multi-world spill on one host — admission control and resource fairness between spilled worlds.

## Scope

- Per-world budgets on a spill host: turn CPU time, concurrent in-flight turns, append submission rate, replay bandwidth. A world over budget is throttled at its own executor; heat alone never revokes a lease.
- Control-traffic priority: renewal submissions and replay catch-up for other worlds schedule ahead of a hot world's mutation submissions, so one world's flood cannot false-expire a neighbour.
- Grant-time admission control: the DO's selection policy treats a host at its holder budget as ineligible; an unplaceable spill waits as pending intent instead of over-committing the host.

## Trigger / gating

**Do not start until trigger T3 fires:** the first host holding (or asked to hold) more than one spilled world, or a #5685 fairness case is run against a spill host. Design: #5787. Composes with: #5685. Depends on: #3805.

## Acceptance

- [ ] The design §7 two-worlds-one-floods case passes: the flooding world is throttled at its budget while the other world's renewal and append latency stay in bound.
- [ ] #5685 fairness-attack cases applicable to a spill host are run and recorded on this issue.
title: id: spill v2 phase 3 — multi-world spill admission control and fairness budgets (#5787)

Its job is research and design — broaden the idea beyond what is already understood, set up multiple next steps, and produce implementation plans. No implementation starts here; the output is design documents and implementation issues.

## Drew's principles for everything in Phase 14 (from #1240, 2026-11-05)
- Local-first is always the goal, AND a hosted version is intended: central coordination supporting a large graph of broadly accessible objects.
- Anything built must be completely usable by others hosting a small or large server themselves. P2P-hosted worlds and data behave the same as a large hosted public server; differences live in backend scale elements and access controls.
- Users connect to each other and transfer/interact directly wherever possible, so hosted resources are an offloadable backstop, not a requirement. The app must not technically need us to function. Collaborative / shared / federated / local-first / p2p.
- Our hosted instance is essentially public; other operators open theirs only as much as they want. Publishing paths: share to a big server, publish on pkarr, or self-host. All comms through iroh on the backend; first-class clients.

Phase 12 makes worlds data; this topic makes the

body:
Found during the 2026-11-07 fleet-wide DB audit + rename/mode-fix program (#6619).

Facts, all empirically verified on scratch DBs (CLI v1.0.33):
- `turso db list` TYPE column is the only mode evidence: `SQLite` = libsql mode, `Turso` = TursoDB mode.
- There is no `turso db rename`.
- A `--from-db` fork INHERITS the source database's type; `turso db create --from-db X --tursodb` fails with "tursodb flag contradicts the database derived type". A fork can never change mode.
- The only working conversion is: `turso db export <db>` -> copy the export files to the target basename -> `turso db import <file>.db --tursodb` (the new DB is named after the FILE basename), then repoint every producer, confirm, and delete the old DB.
- `turso db dump` does not exist in this CLI version (prints help).

Impact: converting the fleet's 8 libsql DBs on 2026-11-07 meant 8 full data moves (~7.7 GB total exports), per-DB token re-mints, and producer flips — for what should be a metadata operation. If Turso ever ships a mode-convert or rename verb, the fleet's remaining libsql holdouts (atlas monolith, great-star-lord — both deliberately untouched, see #6619) should use it. Until then, any new fleet DB must be created with --tursodb at birth; a libsql DB created by accident costs a full migration later.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The rule 'every new fleet Turso DB is created with --tursodb at birth' is recorded in the fleet's DB-creation documentation/runbook where a creator will see it.
- [ ]
title: turso CLI: no rename and no libsql->TursoDB mode conversion — every fix is a full export/import data move

## Coalesce queue claim flow + add a real file-transfer verb (fewer round trips, WS-C census)

Part of epic #5412. Census evidence: WS-C comment on #5701 (2026-11-04). Every sandbox↔laptop round trip costs ~200–600 ms warm, so round-trip COUNT is the lever until/unless the multiplexed-tunnel work lands.

### Round-trip census today (code + logs)
| Operation | Transport round trips | Wall (measured) |
|---|---|---|
| Single trivial exec (`laptop-agent.py exec -- true`) | 1 (unix to session proxy + 1 pooled-tunnel HTTP request) | wall 346–719 ms; trip p50 369 ms |
| `fleet queue claim` (one claim) | 1 (`call("/claim")` → one `broker_roundtrip` → one `unix_roundtrip`; repo-queue crate `crates/repo-queue/src/main.rs` cmd_claim/call) | ~1 trip ≈ 0.3–0.6 s warm |
| Claimant launch flow (claim + lane + bind) | 3 separate CLI invocations = 3 round trips (cmd_lane, cmd_bind are separate `call()`s) | ~1–2 s warm, ×3 failure surfaces |
| Detached job to completion (`run` + `poll` loop) | 1 + N polls (poll sleeps 3 s client-side and re-requests per iteration, laptop-agent.py `poll`) | grows with job length |
| Small file fetch from laptop | NO file verb exists: fetch = 1 exec round trip with `base64 -w0` in a shell string (measured 301 ms wall for /etc/hostname), 1 MiB/stream cap, +33% base64 size, no resume/offsets | 1 trip + encoding overhead |

## Context

The 2026-11-04 nixpkgs update (tracking: #2715) moves `nixpkgs-25` `e7439b6b` -> `1d060086` (the Hydra-gated nixos-unstable channel revision). At the new revision, `haskellPackages.regex-pcre` (pulled into the amd system closure via `haskellPackages.misfortune` in `nixos/environment/default.nix`) is marked broken under nixpkgs' problems framework, and the marking is honest: with the broken flag warned through, its build fails deterministically in the configure phase --

```
Error: [Cabal-7620]
The program 'pkg-config' version >=0.9.0 is required but it could not be found.
```

nixpkgs' Haskell builder no longer adds the `pkg-config` wrapper (or the pkgconfig-depends libraries) to Haskell build environments -- the same mechanism the 2026-10-30 run hit on the master pin (that instance is tracked in #3906). Drew ruled on 2026-11-04 ("fix it or pin misfortune") to revive the #3906-class override for the nixpkgs-25 segment rather than keep the input frozen.

## The temporary override

`nixos/environment/default.nix` extends the raw `nixpkgs-25` legacyPackages segment with an overlay that overrides `haskellPackages.regex-pcre` to append `pkg-config` to its `nativeBuildInputs` and a minimal vendored pcre 8.45 (the version the old pins shipped; test suite disabled) to its `buildInputs`, restoring the old build environment for this one package. A problems handler scoped to `regex-pcre` warns the broken marking through so the overridden derivation can evaluate.

## Removal
title: chore(deps): remove the nixpkgs-25 regex-pcre pkg-config/pcre override once stock regex-pcre builds at the channel rev

Extends #2048 (Zettelkasten layer — multiplayer docs/wiki on ID). This is an EXPANSION design and explicitly **a design to go make designs**: a feature-matrix investigation program whose output is a family of follow-on designs, not one monolithic spec.

## Problem

#2048 establishes the zettelkasten/knowledge layer on ID. Before building further, we need to know — systematically, not anecdotally — what the mature knowledge tools actually do, which of those features cluster into coherent ID designs, and how existing users' content gets in and out. Skipping this risks reinventing a worse Notion while missing the one feature (e.g. the graph, or daily notes) that makes a knowledge tool sticky.

## Method (the program itself)
1. **Enumerate:** for each product below, produce a feature inventory from primary sources (docs, hands-on use): features named consistently so they can be compared across products.
2. **Matrix:** build a product × feature matrix (products as columns, features as rows, with notes on quality/implementation differences, not just yes/no).
3. **Cluster:** group features into coherent clusters; each cluster becomes **one follow-on design ticket** against #2048.
4. **Decide per cluster:** adopt / adapt to ID's multiplayer object model / explicitly reject with reasons. No feature is adopted by default just because a competitor has it.
5. **Import/export designs** (below) proceed in parallel — they depend on the object model in #2048, not on every cluster decision.
title: id: design: Knowledge layer feature program — competitor feature matrix, import/export, read-authority

`secrets/sops/common/bws.yaml` is a full mirror of the Bitwarden vault produced by `lib/bws-to-sops.sh`. It drifted silently once already: by the time #5381 was filed, the mirror was missing 27 current vault keys (including the whole `supabase.muse-dev2.*` set), still carried 10 retired un-namespaced `supabase.*` keys, and had missed 2 value rotations.

Ask: a periodic freshness check so this cannot happen silently again — e.g. a scheduled job (cron or a dispatch-only workflow, respecting the fleet's CI-on-main rules) that runs `lib/bws-to-sops.sh --dry-run`, compares the vault key set against the committed mirror's keys, and on any drift (added / removed / value-changed key names — names only, never values) opens or updates a tracking issue as the app.

## Acceptance criteria
- A scheduled freshness check exists and runs `lib/bws-to-sops.sh --dry-run` (or equivalent key-set comparison) against the committed `secrets/sops/common/bws.yaml`.
- On drift it surfaces the differing key names (never values) in a GitHub issue, filed or updated as the app, with no duplicate issue per drift episode.
- The check is demonstrated once against a deliberately stale mirror (or the current one pre-regeneration state) and once against a fresh mirror, with output linked here.
title: bws.yaml mirror freshness check: periodic bws-to-sops dry-run diff

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 20); parent topic issue: [#5964](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5964). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Precedent

**LambdaMOO feature objects** are the library model Drew described, working since the '90s: create a feature object implementing reusable verbs, and any player object can attach it and gain those commands — libraries as *runtime-attached objects*, no recompilation of the consumer (https://www.moo.mud.org/moo-faq/lcore-getting-started.html).

## Scope

Distinct from the taxonomy child of #5955 (attachment as *classification*: genre/game/entity/none) and from the DLL design (#5964: per-user *functions*): this is runtime attach/detach of *library behavior* to entities inside a running world.

- Attach/detach semantics: who may attach (entity owner, world author), at what moment (tick boundary), what happens to in-flight invocations.
- The attached library's capability footprint composes with the entity's and the world's ceilings — checked how, at attach time?
- Detach and version change: state the library accumulated on the entity — kept, migrated, dropped?

## Done looks like

A design note stating whether feature-object attachment is a v-next mechanism for us, and if so its semantics; if not, the recorded reason.
title: id: design: feature-object library attachment — runtime attach/detach of library behavior to entities without world recompilation

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S36–S38 and S45 of the 2026-11-04 brief. This is the V3 stage of the program.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

User-level code should be passable into a **running world without recompiling the whole world**:

- At least in one version of the compiler there is a way to make a **DLL**. The **server side compiles that DLL itself** — user code is never trusted pre-compiled.
- The platform then **places the DLL in the appropriate location** for the world-side code to call it.
- If a user changes what's running, the world-side code **picks it up as soon as it's compiled and available to be hot-swapped in**.
- **Trust chain:** the server can trust the code because it did the compilation itself; and the only non-pure things the user function can do are from the **server's own platform being passed to it by the world author** — and the world author can trust that chain too.

## Design points to settle

- Interface contract: what signature/shape a user DLL exposes, and how the world discovers and binds it (name, version, interface hash). Mismatch behavior: refuse, fall back to previous version, or run the user's prior published code (see the compile-economics child — "keep running what you'd already published" is the stated default).
- Swap semantics: swap at tick boundary only? In-flight calls finish on the old code — state handoff between versions (the function's state is
title: id: design: dynamic user functions — server-compiled DLLs, hot-swap into running worlds without world recompile

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S17–S18 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Design the system for when a place a user has **already connected to before** changes its capabilities:

- The change may be an **expansion** (strict superset), or a **sideways modification** — not a strict reproduction of the previous capability set.
- **By default there is a warning or notice before the user connects** and has unexpected results. No silent upgrades of what a known world can do.

## Design points to settle

- What is compared: the registry's requested set, the discovered-used set (see the capability-model child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)), or both? A change in *used* with no change in *requested* is exactly the sideways case that matters.
- Notice content: diff presented in plain language (new capabilities named), not a hash change.
- User choices on notice: proceed once, proceed and accept the new set as the baseline, refuse. Is there a "remember for capability decreases only" asymmetry (decreases are safe, increases warn)?
- Who else gets notified: server admins for server-side capabilities, world authors when a library they depend on changes its capability footprint.
- Interaction with invites ([#5751](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5751)): does accepting an invite pin the capability set the invite was issued under?

## Problem

Every PM-stack service keeps its own private data store today:

- aggregator: JSON files in ~/.local/state/pm-aggregator/ (actions, comments, registry, fleet feed, quota state, snapshots/)
- projector: its own SQLite file (~/.local/state/pm-projector/projector.db) — even though its design already namespaces its tables pmp_ precisely so they can live in a shared database (see pm-stack/projector/README.md: the registry fields are name-spaced so they can live in the fleet's existing database rather than requiring a dedicated one)
- Grist: its own document storage for the roadmap table and the registers
- Kaneo, Pad, ready-for-agent: their own stores again

Consequences: cross-service questions (links between projects, issues, roadmap rows; one event stream) need bespoke joins per pair; freshness depends on each service's own polling/restart behavior (see code#1288 for the Grist live-apply problem); backups and restarts are per-service crafts.

## Proposal

Move the stack's service data into ONE database with a shared schema of namespaced table groups:

- One database (libSQL/Turso-shaped, matching the projector's existing storage choice; local file on the laptop with the fleet's existing backup legs) as the single home.
- Table groups per service with clear prefixes (pmp_ projector/link registry, agg_ aggregator stores, plus shared entity tables for items, links, comments, events that more than one service uses).

## Multiplexed persistent streams over ONE tunnel for the sandbox↔laptop path (WS-C design, from #5701)

Part of epic #5412. Design evidence: WS-C connection-performance comment on #5701 (2026-11-04).

### Measured problem (2026-11-04, trips.jsonl n=1149 + live probes)
- Warm single trivial call: client trip p50 369 ms (status-200, <2 s subset, n=800) while daemon work is 1–11 ms (daemon trips.jsonl; example trip aedc705d4294: client 445 ms vs daemon 1 ms). Transport ≈ 99% of cost.
- The path is HTTP/1.1-request-per-call over a pooled CONNECT tunnel (pool 50 in `fleet proxy serve`). Even warm, one request/response costs ~170–600 ms over the runtime-proxy (:3130) + DERP hairpin path. A warm RTT is the floor for EVERY operation, and every CLI operation is a separate call.
- Cold CONNECT measured 1,434 ms trip (same-minute warm trip: 212 ms) — CONNECT setup ≈ 1.2–1.8 s, and the ramp test on #5701 showed CONNECT setup serializes under concurrency (128 tunnels = 14.6 s wall, no failures).
- Failure amplification: during proxy wobble, trips cluster at 502 after ~16.3 s (p50, n=119) and no-status after ~26 s (p50, n=73) — retry chains multiply the herd.

### Proposal
Replace HTTP-per-call over N pooled tunnels with ONE (or two, for redundancy) persistent tunnel carrying multiplexed streams:

1. **Framed stream multiplexer on the tunnel** (the broker already speaks length-prefixed frames on its unix socket — extend that framing end-to-end): each request is a stream (id, port/service,
title: Connection perf: multiplexed persistent streams over one tunnel (replace HTTP-per-call + pool of 50)

## Problem

When a model door stops answering, sessions routed to it stay wedged in a retry loop. They do not fail over to a door that works, and new waves keep being routed to the dead door. Five issues report the same failure, one per door, with 58 to 96 comments each and no code change:

| Issue | Door | Failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #9549 | `_claude` | OAuth renewal answers 429; every session dies at launch |
| #9856 | `_antigravity` | 403, account disabled for terms of service |
| #9859 | `_muse` | 429, weekly window at 100% |
| #9961 | `cline-pass` | 429, monthly limit reached |
| #10085 | `opencode-go` sub-accounts | 429; sessions freeze at retry attempt 2 |

Each was parked on the owner. None needs him: a quota wall resets by itself, and what the fleet controls is whether it keeps sending work into the wall.

## What to build

1. **Measure first.** For each of the five doors, record today's state: answering, walled until a known reset time, or dead.
2. **A walled door is skipped until its reset.** When a door answers with a quota wall that names a reset time, or with an auth failure, the route marks the door unusable until that time (or until a probe succeeds) and stops routing new sessions to it.
3. **A wedged session fails over.** A session whose door fails this way moves to the next door in its route within one retry, or ends with a clear error that the scheduler can re-launch elsewhere. It does not hold a lane while it retries.
4. **Door state is data, not an is

Extends #2036 (ID messaging/relay protocol v1). This is an EXPANSION design: it does not replace #2036, it defines the concrete wire format #2036 assumes and the adapter family that lets ID run where native iroh/UDP cannot.

## Problem

#2036 designs messaging/relay at the protocol level, but leaves open: (a) the exact bytes on the wire, (b) how ID traffic crosses interfaces that cannot natively speak the iroh UDP protocol, and (c) how relays/proxies behave as standard, high-performance infrastructure rather than ad-hoc fallbacks. Without a frozen wire contract, every adapter and every implementation invents its own framing and versioning, and forward compatibility becomes guesswork.

## Goal

One canonical postcard wire schema for ID, versioned and forward-compatible, plus a family of transport adapters that carry the *same* ID payloads unchanged over non-UDP interfaces, with relays and proxies specified as first-class standard protocols.

## Feature set — full expansion

### 1. Canonical postcard wire schema

Extends #5741 (SPLADE investigation + eval harness) and #5668 (query-embed cache + flags). Design commitments from Drew's direction 2026-11-04.

## Principle

**Anything not baked into how data is stored must be settable per query** — from the fleet-binary CLI flags AND from the raw query format (the full-access path), with **identical parameter names** in both — so values can be benchmarked and better defaults found **without editing code**.

If a retrieval constant lives in code today, that's a bug against this principle.

## Knob inventory (v1, extensible)

- **Per-shard top-k** — how many results each shard returns into the fan-out.
- **Global fan-in top-k** — how many combined results survive the merge.
- **Per-signal weights** — dense, BM25, SPLADE (the #5741 adaptive-weighting defaults, overridable per query).
- **Per-signal multipliers** — score scaling per signal, distinct from the weights.
- **Jaccard rescore depth** — candidate count entering the #5733 rescore stage.
- **Jaccard boost threshold** — the overlap at which the rescore boost applies.
- **RRF constant k** — if reciprocal-rank fusion is used in the merge, its k is a knob, never a hardcoded 0.6.
- **Stage toggles** — planner and spell correction off / deprioritized / on (companion issue: query-understanding front-end, extends #5741).
- **Hint override** — force the query class (code / docs / error / concept) instead of the classifier's call.
- **Variant selection** — raw / rewritten / both.
- **Expand-N**
title: atlas search: query-time parameter surface — every retrieval knob as a CLI flag / raw-query field, no hardcoded constants (extends #5741, #5668)

## Summary

Build the **framework** that lets a server, a world, or a user declare and enforce residency and boundary rules — as opt-in capabilities that admins and users can ENABLE, never as defaults imposed on everyone.

This extends and unifies three existing threads: #2283 (jurisdiction-aware hosted stores), #3397 (jurisdiction-partitioned worlds / blobs), and #3398 (residency boundaries for bridge / federation / relays). Those issues each touch one surface. This issue is the shared framework underneath them: what counts as evidence of residency / citizenship, how a boundary is declared, how it is enforced at each surface, and how violations and edge cases behave.

Relates to: #2283, #3397, #3398.

## Priority and framing note (from Drew)

Wanted, but **framework-first and lower urgency**. Do NOT over-index on EU privacy / GDPR-style use cases — they are one possible use of the framework, not its reason to exist and not its design centre.

Two framing rules are hard requirements for every design produced from this issue:

1. **Capabilities, never defaults.** Restrictions are capabilities a server admin or user can enable for their server / world / account. Nothing in this framework turns a restriction on by default, and no deployment inherits a boundary it did not choose.
2. **Basic frameworks first.** Ship the declaration, evidence, and enforcement skeleton in its simplest useful form before any sophisticated policy language, automated classification, or jurisdiction-spe

design: bake the SSH recovery path into the fleet binary

Links: epic #5412 · laptop-agent design #5343
Drew's end state: **no shell scripts, no Python scripts — just the fleet
binary.** This issue covers the *recovery* SSH path only (the daemon-down
escape hatch). The everyday path's Python is the sibling item: the
`fleet laptop-agent` client domain (see Ordering, below).

## Context — the recovery path today (three of our files)

`~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` (the shim) delegates exec-style calls to the
laptop-agent, but shapes the agent cannot express fall back to real SSH.
The fallback classes, from the shim's own header:

- `LAPTOP_SSH_REAL=1` (explicit escape hatch / daemon-down recovery)
- no arguments (interactive session) or a **leading ssh option**
  (`-L/-R/-W/-N/-t/-p/-l/-i/-o …` — forwards and TTY allocation)
- **stdin carrying data** for the remote command (sudo -S feeds,
  `cat > file` pushes) — the daemon has no stdin channel

The fallback is `~/tools/laptop-ssh-real.sh`, which `exec`s system ssh:

```sh
exec ssh \
  -o "ProxyCommand=python3 $HOME/tools/laptop-proxy-connect.py" \
  -o "StrictHostKeyChecking=yes" \
  -o "UserKnownHostsFile=$HOME/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop" \
  -o "IdentitiesOnly=yes" -i "$HOME/.ssh/id_ed25519" \
  -o "ConnectTimeout=60" -o "ConnectionAttempts=3" \
  -o "ServerAliveInterval=15" -o "ServerAliveCountMax=8" \
  -o "ControlMaster=auto" -o "ControlPath=$HOME/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p" \
  -o "ControlPersist=3600" \
  "user@100.99.113.103" "$@"
```

…a

Part of epic #1184; implementation follow-up of design issue #1259 (spend rollups). Design note: `doc/spend-rollups-design-1259.md`. Depends on the rollup-store slice of #1259.

## Scope
Detect cost anomalies from the spend rollups and surface them through the existing alert throat (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/alerts.ts`, #3676) into Needs-you (/attention) and the Today/brief summary — no new notification path.

## Anomaly classes (v1, thresholds are named constants with tests, per the design note)
- **Burn without progress:** an epic/project consumes spend in a window while closing zero child issues in the same window.
- **Single-session dominance:** one root session accounts for more than the threshold share of an epic's window spend.
- **Unattributed growth:** the unattributed share of total spend rises window-over-window beyond the threshold.
- **Charge without activity:** a matched PAYG charge for a service with no corresponding session/quota activity in its period.

## Rules
- Missing or partial data suppresses the anomaly, never fabricates it: an anomaly needs a complete window on both sides of its comparison.
- Each surfaced anomaly names its evidence: scope, window, the two compared values, and a link to the rollup/drill-down.
- Delivery class: page + ledger (warning) in v1; no push, per the alerts design (warnings never push in v1).

## Acceptance criteria
- One test per anomaly class: fires on the constructed pattern, silent on partial data, silent just below threshol

The Supabase backup staging uploads (`supabase-backups` bucket, `pg/muse-dev/staging/` prefix, written by `supabase_backup.py` from the laptop) leak **incomplete multipart uploads** when an upload fails or is interrupted: the staging object is retried under a new key and the failed upload is never aborted.

Implements the accepted design from #2818. See the design note `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2818.md` and design PR #3875.

Build the journaled handoff for an application-owned entity crossing between spatial region shard-worlds. Use dedicated source/destination journal entries plus coordinator open/close records. The required local order is prepare/validate → persist typed record → apply in-memory state → acknowledge. Keep region journals independent; do not emulate a cross-region transaction or put entity payloads in the coordinator journal.

## Phased packets

1. **Journal/schema/checkpoint foundation** — typed handoff records, entity-addressed input, world journal version 3 bump/rollback compatibility, and compaction preservation for active handoffs, epochs, tombstones, and receipts.
2. **Program contract + source export/fence** — pure `prepare_entity_transfer` hook, region-sharded mode gate, complete bounded entity payload, persist-before-apply source record, and source-side stale-write rejection. No receipt until apply/replay succeeds.
3. **Destination import** — module/schema/digest validation, persist-before-apply import, idempotency by handoff ID, durable receipt only after apply/replay, and failure tests.
4. **Coordinator/recovery** — journal start and observed receipts, retry/reconcile after crashes, and region-map switch only after matching durable receipts and a durable completion record.
5. **Client/operations** — explicit transit/stuck status, fail-closed entity rea

Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — wave 2, 2026-10-26).

The stack's sources disagree regularly — Project Status vs the aggregator's derived state, Kaneo card state vs GitHub issue state — and today each disagreement lives where it happens to render: a ⚠ badge on /projects, invisible everywhere else, with no way to resolve the class of problem, only the instance. A source-conflict inbox collects every live disagreement into one queue: each entry names the item, the two sources, both values, and how long they have disagreed. Drew (or the orchestrator, for classes Drew has ruled on) records a per-class ruling — "for Kaneo-vs-GitHub state, trust GitHub" — and the ruling applies to that class going forward, recorded as data (not code), until changed. Resolved classes stop generating inbox entries; a source that starts disagreeing in a new way creates a new class rather than re-opening an old ruling silently.

Acceptance:
- One page lists all current source disagreements across facets (not only /projects), each with item, sources, both values, and disagreement age.
- A per-class "trust source X" ruling can be recorded, is stored as data, and measurably suppresses that class's entries while applying the trusted value in renders.
- Rulings are listed and revocable in the same place; revoking re-surfaces the class's current disagreements.
- The inbox count appears in the stack health surface so a growing conflict backlog is itself visible; covered by tests with seeded disagreem

## Summary

Expand #2046 (serverless edition — `id` on Cloudflare Workers) with the storage decision it left open: what is the backing store for `id` when it runs on Workers, and can the answer be more than one store?

This is a design investigation, not an implementation ticket. Its deliverable is a decision-ready comparison of **Cloudflare D1 vs Turso (libSQL) vs offering both**, a recommendation with the conditions that would flip it, and follow-on design tickets (see Decomposition sketch) detailed enough to be broken into implementation work without re-litigating the choice.

Relates to: #2046 (serverless edition on Cloudflare Workers), #806 (F12.13 journal replication — read replicas over a signed stream).

## Why this matters

The serverless edition promises `id` with no server to run. That promise lives or dies on the store underneath it:

- Every `id` invariant — identity, capability grants, journal / event history, world state — has to survive on a store whose consistency, replication, and failure model were designed for edge web apps, not necessarily for a signed, replicated journal.
- Picking the wrong store does not just cost performance; it can silently weaken the journal's guarantees (ordering, durability, replay) or lock the serverless edition into a cost / limits shape that only appears at scale.
- Conversely, supporting two stores doubles the storage-abstraction surface forever. "Both" must be justified, bounded, and priced — not adopted as an avoidance of de
title: design(id): serverless edition storage — D1 vs Turso vs both for `id` on Cloudflare Workers

Relocated from dezren39/nix#6 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): mcpx's single source lives in developing-today/code (pkgs/mcpx); re-home tracked at #309. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

Parent: #181

## Idea

Record everything mcpx and its harness learn as events in one table, so that
any statistic is a query rather than a new code path.

Today `mcpx stats` has seven dimensions and `mcpx stats --opencode` has six,
each a hand-written query against a differently-shaped source. Adding a source
— a REST API, a hosted mcpx, a second harness — means writing that set again.

## Shape

```sql
CREATE TABLE event (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  ts_unix_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
  kind_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES kind(id),
  idset_id   INTEGER REFERENCES idset(id),   -- who/what this concerns
  source     TEXT NOT NULL,                  -- mcpx, opencode, rest, tui
  value      REAL,                           -- the number, when there is one
  data       TEXT                            -- the rest, as JSON
);
```

### Identifier sets

The repeated shape is "this event concerns session X, whose parent is Y, in
worktree Z". Those combinations recur constantly, so interning them is both a
large space saving and what makes `GROUP BY idset_id` mean something.

```sql
CREATE TABLE idset (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, fingerprint TEXT UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE idset_member (idset_id INTEGER, key TEXT, value TEXT,
title: Event store: one table for every statistic, from any source

## What this is

#alignment (C0CBYQR65LL) is the agent coordination channel. Aster is in it and proposed the channel contract on 2026-10-28 (verified senders; every dispatch carries ID/owner/scope/evidence; ACK/BLOCKED then RESULT in-thread; dedupe; no credentials). OpenClaw is not in it yet — its bot binding and delivery are unverified. Drew asked 2026-10-29 to add OpenClaw and to settle whether one channel for all agents is enough, or each pair needs its own point-to-point path.

## The topology question

**One shared channel** (recommended):
- Channels stay O(1) as agents are added; pairwise grows O(n^2).
- Every dispatch and result sits in one record — the OpenClaw/OpenCode review needs to see traffic it was not part of.
- Threads per dispatch keep it readable; the contract keeps it disciplined.

**Point-to-point per pair**:
- Wins only for high-volume pair traffic, or content that should not be visible to the other agents.
- Costs: fragmented record, hidden context, and N^2 channels to babysit as the roster grows (Muse, Aster, OpenClaw, OpenCode today; more coming).

Recommendation: one shared #alignment for all dispatch and results, one thread per dispatch ID, contract as Aster proposed. Add a point-to-point path only when a specific pair proves it needs one (volume or sensitivity), and record that exception here.

In the #2050 design every downloader becomes a useful partial holder the moment its first chunk group verifies — FsStore persists verified ranges, and bao verification makes a partial holder's ranges exactly as trustworthy as a complete holder's. **Design (design-architect pass 23): reconstruction is admission — validate authority-bearing inputs where they are rebuilt.**

Design doc: `files/designs/code-id-reconstruction-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audited against origin/main `206f4fd7`.

## Summary

Six issues filed independently in one evening are one defect with six addresses: in `pkgs/id`, data that carries authority is validated when it is created live, and trusted when it is reconstructed — a world journal being restored, an attestation being computed from decoded objects, a manifest being parsed, a schedule cap being checked. The live path enforces invariants (only issued, JOIN-holding participants act; claims answer the agreement they name; a manifest step means what it says); the reconstruction paths enforce almost none of them, so a crafted or corrupted artefact acquires authority the live path would never have granted.

**The recorded rule:** reconstruction is admission. Anywhere `pkgs/id` rebuilds authority-bearing state from stored or supplied data, the rebuilding code validates the same invariants the live path enforces at creation, and refuses (never partially applies, never silently repairs) data that violates them. Corollaries: validate against state you hold, not claims the input makes; unnamed means refused (scope bits, manifest keys, outcomes); the system shape (sequence 0 / participant 0) is not borrowable by authority-carrying entries.

You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

Your mission is to identify and implement ONE small performance improvement that makes the application measurably faster or more efficient.

✅ **Always do:**

- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

- Make breaking changes
- Optimize prematurely without actual bottleneck
- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson

- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine

## Proposal
- User names n guardians (existing ID contacts) + threshold m; the set is a keyset record.
- Recovery: a new keypair publishes a recovery request (directory layer); m guardians sign approvals; the assembled rotation record installs the new key after a **delay window** during which the old key can cancel with one signature and all devices/bindings are notified.
- Adding a guardian is instant; removing one is itself delayed (anti-evict-then-attack).

## Acceptance
- [ ] Guardian set record + approval/rotation record formats specified against the keyset log.
- [ ] Delay + cancel + notify flow implemented with tests, including the guardian-eviction attack case.
- [ ] Server role is relay/timestamp only; no approval can be forged or the delay shortened server-side.
title: id: guardian social recovery — threshold approvals + delayed, cancellable key rotation

## Symptom
After the laptop's 2026-11-16 ~05:35–05:39 CT outage and recovery, `gnome-keyring-daemon` restarted (05:38) outside a desktop login session and stayed **locked**. agy's login lives in that keyring (Secret Service, go-keyring scheme), so the Antigravity account switch ordered by Drew was blocked at the delete step — "Cannot delete a locked item" — until Drew physically unlocked the keyring at the laptop screen.

## Why it should not happen
The keyring normally unlocks via PAM at desktop login. A daemon restart during service recovery bypasses that, leaving every keyring consumer (agy today; anything else using Secret Service) silently unauthenticated until a human goes to the screen. Drew's position: "it should unlock itself."

## Scope
- Make keyring unlock survive daemon/service restarts on the laptop: e.g. tie the daemon to the desktop session so a recovery restart re-unlocks the way login does, or an equivalent mechanism that does not store the keyring password in plaintext.
- Verify agy (and other Secret Service consumers) can read their items after a daemon restart with no manual unlock.

## Acceptance check
Restart gnome-keyring-daemon out-of-session (simulating the recovery path), then confirm `agy --print` authenticates with no unlock prompt and no manual step.

## Refs
- Surfaced 2026-11-16 during the agy popesdrew switch (drewrypope account is ToS-disabled, see #9856).
title: laptop keyring stays locked after daemon restart — Secret Service consumers (agy) blocked until manual unlock

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S66–S72 of the 2026-11-04 brief. Extends the presentation-tiers design in [#786](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/786) — that issue covers capability tiers with in-band terminal detection; this one covers user-supplied assets and filters living on top of the tiers.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

- In the future, users might provide **GPU shaders**, and **images or sprites that were uploaded already as a given ID**.
- A user will be able to **set their sprite to have a cape and apply the filter "sparkle" to the cape** — **without any of that being specifically coded by a given app**.
- This is an **imperfect system**, and the **app would have to enable such capabilities**.
- Over time there may become a **common interface for different formats** and **basic conversion tools at the presentation layer**, to allow this to work on a **variety of devices** and a **variety of worlds**, which may or may not support different capabilities.
- **Per-world gating:** one world might not support filters, because you could make yourself look like a different kind of creature, or make a filter that basically **makes you invisible** — so it's **just disabled in this world**.
- **Graceful fallback is authored, not improvised:** "when filters are disabled, put static sparkles on the GIF image of my sprite."
- **Terminal degradation:** another user viewing on a termi
title: id: design: user presentation assets — shaders, sprites by ID, filters, per-world gating, graceful degradation

## Direction (Drew, 2026-10-31)

Atlas moves from a single canonical DB + one Turso publish to provenance-first, scalable infrastructure. Design doc: hatch-personal `workspace/turso-atlas/docs/atlas-provenance-and-scale-design-2026-10-31.md`.

Rules:
1. Keep ALL data — nothing stripped from atlas.db or publishes to save space; only byte-identical dupes are cleaned, backups kept.
2. Backups AND plain extracts for every corpus.
3. Every chunk records EVERY place it was found: `chunk_occurrences` (chunk → array of source locators with spans, observed_at). Today dedup silently drops occurrences (~127K at first ingest); 6,344 canonical sessions own zero chunks for exactly this reason and their occurrences are unrecorded.
4. Every import is interned content-addressed (laptop extracts CAS / R2, registry maps CA hash → normal paths) or pinned as `repo@commit:path`. Registry also holds line numbers / dates / spans for extracts.
5. Retrieval: vector/FTS search across multiple Turso shard DBs (collection × month) returns IDs; a catalog/registry resolves an ID to a file, a chunk, or a start–end section — including a member of a tar in R2 (sidecar index, range fetch) or a local file.

Verified state feeding this (2026-10-31): canonical 18,325 sessions / 122,124 messages / 107,639 chunks; local-only = 6,941 chunks of personal-client TEXT held back from Turso by policy (not missing embeddings); Turso atlas 1.0 GB / 100,698 chunks; laptop ~/atlas 12 GB contains NO consequential byte-identica
title: atlas: provenance registry (chunk occurrences), content-addressed extracts, multi-DB vector resolution

## Problem: home IPv6 uplink stalls on real transfers

Diagnosed 2026-10-26 during the OpenClaw install work on the amd laptop.

**Symptom:** IPv6 connections to Cloudflare-fronted hosts (e.g. registry.npmjs.org) stall at zero bytes on payload-sized responses, while IPv4 to the same hosts is healthy (~530 KB/s).

Evidence (on amd, home network):
- `curl -6` of a ~4 MB npm tarball: 0 bytes after ~22 s (hard stall, not slowness).
- `curl -4` of the same tarball: full download in ~8 s.
- Interactive tools with happy-eyeballs (curl default) mask the problem by falling back to IPv4; node/pnpm does not fall back the same way, so nix fixed-output fetches for npm/pnpm deps repeatedly stalled mid-build (notably the ~780-package summarize pnpm-deps FOD), while shell tests looked fine.

## Impact

- npm/pnpm fetches from Nix builds on home machines are unreliable/slow.
- Any IPv6-first client without robust fallback can hang on this network.

## Workaround in place

- IPv4 precedence via `networking.getaddrinfo` in the amd host config (precedence ::ffff:0:0/96 = 100), marked as temporary.
- Prefer-IPv4 choices in ad-hoc tooling until this is fixed.

## What "fixed" means

Find and repair the root cause on the home network. Suspects, in order:
1. PMTUD black hole on the IPv6 path (large packets dropped; small handshakes succeed — matches the 0-byte-after-connect shape).
2. Router/ONT IPv6 handling (prefix delegation, RA/MTU advertisement, firmware).
3. ISP IPv6 routing/peering toward Clo
title: Home network: IPv6 uplink stalls on payload transfers (PMTUD/router/ISP)

Program epic. Drew ruled **"b and c"** on 2026-11-04 (dezren39/hatch-personal#21): Atlas search ships as **(b)** a Rust binary vendored from this repo and **(c)** a multi-client search service built on that binary.

**Design of record:** `doc/2026-11-04T08-07-13Z_design_atlas_binary_service/` (PR #5348, merged `9c5976340`). Read it before working any step — the decisions below are summaries, the note is the authority.

**Headline decisions**
- One Rust binary (`atlas-search`, `pkgs/atlas-search/`), two modes: standalone-capable one-shot CLI + `serve`. Never thin-client-only.
- Service protocol: HTTP+JSON jobs; branch workers concurrent; fused rankings in an in-memory TTL temp store behind per-job capability tokens; fetch-to-fill escalation lives inside the vector branch, paging slices an immutable ranking.
- Auth: per-client bearer tokens in `~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json`, each carrying a **maximum sensitivity ceiling the server clamps to**. Named clients only; Aster is not a v1 client. Loopback + tailscale serve (MagicDNS), never public.
- Vector backend is a pluggable strategy (`scan` / `index-fill` / `index-fixed`); the golden-311 A/B running on the Python decides the default (design Gate C).
- The Python CLI stays the eval reference permanently and the runtime fallback through cutover. Migration is additive-first; there is no data migration (the system is read-only end to end).

**Program gates** (design §5): Gate A embedder bit-identity on the probe set; Gate
title: Epic: Atlas as a Rust binary + multi-client search service (b+c)

# Session dispatch + babysitting (OpenChamber program)

## Purpose
Move the fleet's larger code work off Claude cron shifts — whose every turn re-buys a large context — onto OpenChamber-hosted OpenCode sessions running on plan pools, watched by ONE babysitter worker instead of one worker per issue. Design record: `openchamber-dispatch-babysitter-design-2026-10-26.md` (keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace, files/).

## Scope
- **Locations abstraction:** a session executor is a location (kind: openchamber | opencode-server | openclaw | codex-aster) with an adapter + capacity, so more OpenChamber machines, an OpenClaw gateway, or a Codex `.aster` route plug in without changing the babysitter loop. First location: the laptop's OpenChamber.
- **Dispatcher with admission control:** hands queue tasks marked `executor: openchamber` to sessions only when a slot is free and the routed pool passes the quota measurement gate; otherwise hands the task back (parked `executor-saturated`, noted on the issue) — never a silent backlog.
- **One babysitter:** rounds over every bound session — progress verdicts, one stall nudge then escalation, quota walls as named parks, harvesting finished sessions into verified terminal queue states. Reports quota per pool and a routing ledger (pool used per session, escalations, burn per landed task).
- **Routing, Workhorse-first:** Fast / Workhorse (default) / Frontier tiers per the POOL MAP; Frontier only on evidence or for the design half of a split

Design doc: `files/designs/code-mcpx-bounded-response-reads.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audit at origin/main `f93e6dc5b` — every defect below re-verified present at the cited lines this pass (2026-11-02).

## Summary

mcpx reads responses from endpoints it does not control — third-party MCP servers, configured model providers, remote embeddings services — with no byte bound in four places. A client timeout bounds *duration*, never *bytes*: a fast endpoint can deliver gigabytes inside the timeout. Each filing re-derived the same missing rule in a different package:

- **Daemon chat-completions proxy** — `proxyToUpstream` (`internal/daemon/routes_proxy.go:244`) uses `http.DefaultClient` (no deadline at all) and streams the response through a `TeeReader` into an unbounded `bytes.Buffer` kept as the feedback record (#2114; implementation PR #3380 in flight).
- **MCP client non-JSON fallback** — `HTTPTransport.Send` (`internal/mcpclient/http.go:218`) does `io.ReadAll(resp.Body)` uncapped and pushes the result as one "message", while the non-2xx path in the same function caps at 4 KB (#4282).
- **Both OpenAI-compatible providers** — `internal/model/openai.go:123` and `internal/scripting/provider.go:121` buffer whole; on non-2xx the entire body is embedded in the error (#4354; probe: a 32 MiB error body produced a 33.5 MB error string). The `baseURL` is configuration (OpenAI, a company gateway, LiteLLM, Ollama, LM Studio).
- **A fifth instance is unfiled**
title: Design: read it bounded — one response-read contract for mcpx's outbound calls

Implements the policy + federation layers of the owner decision on #185 (comment 6486250456, Drew, 2026-10-28). Likely splits into smaller issues; filed whole so the design stays in one place. Depends on the marker + default-view work (tag.clear as a role-aware marker).

## Pieces
1. **Delete requests.** A first-class operation: anyone can request deletion of a tag, carrying a reason. The request is delivered to the relevant authority holders — the tag's author, group admins, or server owners — and their grant/decline is recorded.
2. **Server delete policies.** A server admin can set policies on their own server that actually delete based on clear markers (and/or granted delete requests). Conditions are the server's business; nothing here is protocol-mandated. Deletes are events (auditable), not silent state edits.
3. **Federated deletes (opt-in per server owner, never default).**
   - A server owner may replicate deletes from federated co-servers.
   - A server owner may accept delete events from ANY server provided the delete is signed by the author or admins and the full chain validates; an invalid or incomplete chain means the foreign delete is not honored.

## Acceptance
- Delete request round-trips: request with reason -> delivered to author/admins/server owners -> grant produces a delete under the server's policy, decline is recorded with no delete.
- A server with no delete policy never hard-deletes from clear markers alone.

Extends #5741 (SPLADE investigation + eval harness + adaptive weighting). Design commitments from Drew's direction 2026-11-04.

## What this adds

Two NEW front-end stages in front of retrieval, each independently toggleable (**off / deprioritized / on**), in pipeline order:

**spell correction → query planner/rewriter → signal weighting (#5741) → fan-out**

## Stage 1 — spell correction

Neither BM25 nor SPLADE tolerates typos: both match on exact terms. The mechanism is classical, not learned:

- **Candidate generation** by Damerau–Levenshtein edit distance (a transposition — flipped letters — counts as 1 edit) plus **character-trigram similarity** (set overlap over character 3-grams; the Jaccard family already in the stack per #5733).
- Candidates are drawn from a **corpus-vocabulary dictionary with term frequencies**, so corrections prefer terms the corpus actually contains.
- Correction is **conservative — high-confidence only**. The original query is **always retained as a variant**; a correction is never silently substituted. The raw and corrected forms can both fan out and merge like any other variant (see dual submission below).

## Stage 2 — query planner / rewriter

A small, fast model rephrases/expands the query into a retrieval-shaped variant: vocabulary the corpus would use, expansions of abbreviations, decomposed compound questions.

- **Dual submission is the default shape**: raw and rewritten both fan out; results merge with **provenance tags** (`raw-only` /
title: atlas search: query-understanding front-end — spell correction + LLM query planner/rewriter as toggleable stages, dual submission with provenance (extends #5741)
