```json
## Direction (Drew, 2026-10-28)

Reviewing the #437 decision, Drew's ruling: systemd socket activation — systemd holds the port across service restarts so connections queue instead of being refused — 'should be what we do for everything', and asked why it isn't already the pattern across the board.

## Verified current state (2026-10-28, flake at laptop ~/git/code)

Exactly ONE service does this today: OpenChamber (`systemd.user.sockets.openchamber`, `ListenStream 127.0.0.1:3000`, home/common/default.nix:999). A grep of the flake finds no other socket units, no `LISTEN_FDS` consumers, and no socket-proxyd anywhere. Everything else binds its own port and refuses connections while it restarts:

- PM stack: pm-aggregator (:4870), pm-projector (:7801) — plain systemd services.
- PM apps (Postgres, Kaneo, Grist, Pad) — Docker containers (compose today, oci-containers once #1762 lands); containers cannot inherit a systemd socket fd the same way.
- OpenCode server (laptop :13420 / tailnet serve :4096) — plain user service.
- OpenClaw gateway (:18789) — plain user service.
- cloudflared, id-mail services — to be inventoried.

## Honest constraint (why this is an audit, not a blanket flip)

Socket activation only works when the program can accept a socket handed to it by systemd (the `LISTEN_FDS` protocol — trivial shim for our own Node services, supported natively by many daemons) or when a proxy shim (systemd-socket-proxyd) in front is acceptable, which adds a hop and its own failur
title: Audit: socket activation as the default pattern for laptop services

Follow-up from the #2065 design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-10-00Z_design_refundable_grants_pending_transfers/`, PR #2293), §6.3.

## Why

The pending-transfer mechanism adds failure modes the posted design did not have: a service that dies between reserve and vest leaves the user's paid grant to expire on the TigerBeetle `timeout`, and a crash between writing intent and submitting the transfer leaves a row whose state disagrees with the ledger.

## Scope

- Sweeper: `state=pending AND window_ends_at < now` → post (retry with backoff), then mark `posted`; `Expired` is a reconcilable state, not a loss.
- Safety net: `timeout` = window + slack (design recommends +72h) so a dead service cannot hold a grant forever; the sweeper must post before that, and the slack is a last resort.
- Drift alarm: compare each grant's `pending_transfer_id` resolution in TigerBeetle against the row state; mismatch is an alert (never a silent fix).
- Late-refund fallback per §6.2: clawback attempt, on `exceeds_credits` mark the grant `debt` and expose it to the gateway's grant/redemption refusal.
- Metrics: pending count, oldest pending age, expired-then-reconciled count, drift count, debt total.

## Depends on

The grant service issue (creates the table and endpoints this reads).

## Done when

A test cluster with a killed service between reserve and vest self-heals via the sweeper, a seeded drift row raises an alarm, and an after-vest refund lands in `debt` rather than throwing.
```

**Design scope only — no data moves in this issue's first pass.**

## What moves
- From: Supabase (`muse-dev2`) `ci.events` (10,952 live rows, 31.8 MB — ~2.9 KB/row of jsonb webhook payload)
- To: Turso, staging tier, partitioned by day/repo

## Why
A pure append-only CI webhook ledger: 10,957 inserts / 0 updates in the stats window since 2026-10-29, no foreign keys, read by scan (its one view, `ci.recent_failures`, is a filtered scan). It is the fastest-growing table in the project by bytes and has no transactional consumer — under the §9 placement rule it is a Turso stream, not Postgres state.

Design doc: §9 of `doc/2026-11-04T21-27-34Z_design_atlas_scaler_revision/` (PR #5667, addendum PR #5689).

## Risks
- The webhook receiver is a live write path — cutover must not drop events during deploys (receiver-side buffering or dual-write).
- `recent_failures` consumers (alerting? dashboards?) must be inventoried first; failure-visibility must not regress during the move.
- Retention is currently unbounded; the Turso design should state a retention window rather than replicating unbounded growth.

## Sketch of steps
1. Inventory the receiver(s) and every reader of `ci.events` / `ci.recent_failures`.
2. Design the Turso table + a `recent_failures`-equivalent query; set retention (propose 90 days hot, cold export beyond).
3. Dual-write at the receiver, backfill the retention window, diff failure queries.
4. Flip readers, stop the Postgres write, keep the Postgres table read-only
title: design: move ci.events webhook ledger from Supabase to Turso staging

Follow-up from the key-recovery investigation on #2060 (doc: `investigations/key-recovery.md` in the ID program workspace, §1/§3/§7). Parent epic: #2056.

## Problem
`pkgs/id` identity is a single Iroh Ed25519 secret key (`src/local.rs`: `SecretKey::generate()` / `open_with_key`); the public key IS the account (invites name it directly, `src/invite.rs`). There is no indirection for device keys, revocation, IdP bindings, or rotations — so a lost key is a lost identity and a second device is a second account.

## Proposal
Design (then implement) a signed keyset/authorization log as the identity substrate: an identity identifier plus an append-only chain of signed records — device-key enrolment/revocation, hosted IdP claim bindings (#2044 §4.3 option 1), guardian sets (see social-recovery follow-up), and key rotations. Group membership and directory records bind to the identity, not to one key. Keyset-admin operations (add/revoke device, change guardians) are narrower-scoped than everyday signing.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Design doc section or ADR covering record formats, fold/verification rules, and the identity identifier derivation.
- [ ] Enrolment + revocation of a second device key via QR/invite-style pairing (`src/qr.rs`, `src/invite.rs` surfaces exist).
- [ ] Existing group-encryption per-device sessions (`src/encryption/`) consume device keys from the keyset.
- [ ] Old single-key accounts migrate via a genesis keyset record signed by the existing key.
title: id: keyset/authorization log — device keys, revocation, bindings as signed records (identity substrate)

Implementation for the design in [#2013](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2013) — design record: [`doc/2026-10-29T10-08-00Z_design_github-content-creation-pacing/`](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/2226) (PR #2226).

## Problem

Every fleet lane authenticates as one account, so GitHub's content-creation ceiling (documented: ~80/min, 500/hour) is a single shared budget no job can see. On 2026-10-28 `developing-today/code` alone produced 2 916 content-creating events (479 issues/PRs + 2 437 comments), peaking at 511 in the 22:00Z hour; creation then stopped for 31m48s after #1999. `gh issue create` exited 0 with empty output while creating nothing, so no caller noticed.

## Scope

Code lands with the fleet tooling (`~/hatch/tools`, `repo-queue.py`, producer/filing scripts), not in this repository. This issue is the tracking record and the spec pointer.

1. **Creation ledger** — `~/.local/state/fleet/content-ledger.sqlite`, one row per content-creating call (`ts_utc, actor, job, repo, kind, ref, outcome`), written as a reservation before the call and finalised after the verifying read; windows computed from the ledger (60 s, 3 600 s), atomic across processes via `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`.
2. **Throttle wrapper** — `reserve(job, kind)` before every create. Account-wide 45/min and 300/hour; ≥ 1 s between POSTs; ≤ 8 in flight; per-lane 50/hour sustained with idle share reclaimable; 75/hour reserve for priority-10 breakage work; bulk programs ≤ 20 issues per 30-m
title: impl: fleet content-creation throttle — shared ledger, pacing budgets, and verify-by-read filing

# Queue fleet reliability

## Purpose
The queue system that keeps the four repos healthy (Supabase `agent.tasks`, the repo-health queues, lane shifts, the fleet monitor) proved itself on 2026-10-26 — and showed exactly two reliability defects. This epic closes both, so the fleet runs for a week at a time without operator repairs.

## Scope
1. **Claim evaporation on the non-code queues.** The code queue runs two staggered lane shifts (~90-min budgets); opencode/openchamber/nix are worked by short-budget arrangements whose runs end mid-task, stranding claims. On 2026-10-26 the monitor repaired 10+ divergences and two tasks died in queue (repaired by operator cap raises + migration 0012's park/resume accounting fix). Child: #1130 — lane-style long-budget shifts for the non-code queues.
2. **Uncertified shift runs.** Five runs on 2026-10-26 ended with a tool result lost, unable to certify their own completion even when the work landed; the parent re-verified from GitHub/queue state by hand each time. Child: #1131 — certify completion from durable state, automatically.

Out of scope: producer jobs (new-issue-creator, pr-diff-review) and the Phase 3 sweep-producer expansion (paused by Drew 2026-10-26; separate decision).

## Execution mode
Online: cron job bodies, worker instructions, monitor duties, Supabase migrations. All changes follow the fleet's isolation rules (pilot functions only; global claim/fail untouched) and the no-uncommitted-code rule.

## Dependencies
Builds on mig
title: epic(fleet): queue fleet reliability — lane workers for every queue, certified shift reporting

body: **Track B.** Reliability core (charter §§13–15; proposal §13): atomic claims issuing lease_token, lease_expiration, session_id, and a fencing/version counter — a stale agent cannot overwrite a newer claim; checkpoints + expiry enable interrupted-session recovery; ownership, execution, and GitHub state remain distinct. Transactional outbox: authoritative local state + durable outbox intent committed atomically; external writes delivered, checked, acknowledged later; states pending / delivering / confirmed / retryable_failure / conflict / terminal_failure; stable operation IDs, remote IDs, expected versions; verify-before-retry so retries never duplicate GitHub comments or repeat merges; no pretense that GitHub and the local DB share an atomic transaction. Direct verified completion: `fleet work complete <id> --merge-pr … --close-issues … --close-queue --require-clean-reconciliation --verify --wait` — validates lease/auth, dependencies, last-minute external activity, PR head SHA, checks/reviews, merge eligibility; moves to completing, persists outbox ops, merges, verifies merge, closes issues, verifies closure, closes the queue item DIRECTLY (no webhook/sweeper dependency for Fleet-initiated completion), records outcome, releases lease. Partial effects (merge ok, closure failed) keep a recoverable completing state and report precisely. title: design(pm-orchestration): leases, fencing, transactional outbox & direct verified completion

## Problem
Retrieval in `pkgs/id` is single-source: `src/commands/get.rs` does one `store.remote().fetch(conn, hash)` over one connection. iroh-blobs (0.103, in Cargo.toml) already supports the swarm-shaped pieces — `(hash, ChunkRanges)` requests per provider, bao verified streaming (each 16 KiB chunk group verified against the blob's BLAKE3 root hash as it arrives, from any source, in any order), partial-blob state in FsStore, and providers reporting the exact missing location when they close a stream for data they lack. What is done late is done in the order the owner did it, with one case left out.

**What holds today.** On the device a later action about the same thing (the same issue, task, reference or set of questions) waits behind an earlier one that has not been taken (`subject` in `pm-stack/console/public/outbox.js`). At the edge, an action that may be held goes behind an earlier one about the same thing that a machine has not taken yet, even when the machine can be reached again (`subjectOf` in `src/edge-proto.ts`, used in the act route of `edge/src/edge.ts`).

**What is left out.** An older action is held for a machine (it was relayed while the edge was not doing that kind itself, or was turned away), and then the edge does a newer one about the same thing itself. The machine does the older one when it is back, and for a kind where the last one wins (`issue.rank`) the older rank replaces the newer.

How to get there: with the laptop away and the edge's token turned away for writes, rank an issue (held for the laptop); press "Try again now" on the Cloudflare screen so the edge takes the kind back; rank the same issue again (done by the edge); bring the laptop back. The issue ends at the first rank.

**What done looks like.**

- When the edge does a kind itself and something older about the same thing is held for a machine and has never been handed to one, the edge does the older one itself first, under its name, and drops it from what is held; or, for a kind where the last one wins,

```
Checking runtime dependencies for awscli-1.44.21-py3-none-any.whl
  - botocore==1.42.31 not satisfied by version 1.43.79
  - s3transfer<0.17.0,>=0.16.0 not satisfied by version 0.19.2
```

awscli 1.44.21 pins botocore exactly and s3transfer to the 0.16 line, but every current pin (master/unstable/stable/25 alike) ships botocore 1.43.79 and s3transfer 0.19.2 — the tree is mid-transition (libraries bumped, awscli not yet). The skew is in the raw sets too, not an artifact of this repo's overlays. awscli and botocore are developed in lockstep (awscli imports botocore internals), so relaxing awscli's pins (pythonRelaxDeps) risks shipping a subtly broken CLI; pinning the libraries back for awscli only is the conservative fix.

An overlay in `nixos/nixpkgs/default.nix` (next to the patchelf override) overrides `awscli` to use dedicated botocore 1.42.31 and s3transfer 0.16.0 derivations (the set's own expressions with version/source rolled back), leaving the set's botocore/s3transfer at their current versions for all other consumers (boto3 etc.).

Defect #7610 (CLOSED): Kaneo's GitHub integration closed issues seconds after Refs-only PR merges. Root causes were structural, not a single bad setting:

Parent: #9093 (backup mesh) · Program: #8983 · Design: `doc/2026-11-23T16-34-18Z_design_backup_mesh/note.md` (landed with the #9093 design PR).
House rules: any schedule this creates lands its `doc/fleet-schedule-registry.md` row in the same PR; secrets by name only (Bitwarden at runtime, repo-archive pattern); builds/tests run via remote dispatch, never on the laptop or sandbox.

## Scope
The embedding stores ride the mesh: the Atlas vector tables / shard databases (the embedding corpora under the atlas-search shard layout) are snapshotted by the same Turso→R2 restic legs as their parent databases, and — the point of this issue — a restore is proven to rebuild search **without a re-embed pass**. Embeddings are the most expensive data in the fleet to recompute; a backup that restores rows but loses or invalidates the embedding store fails the mesh's purpose.

## Terms (from the design)
- No separate embedding backup system: shard DBs are class-B (or class-A where the design names them) members of the rotation like any other Turso DB. This issue owns the *verification* that they are in fact enumerated (the rotation enumerates from `turso db list`, so any shard DB living outside Turso is a named exception handled here).
- Any embedding data living outside a Turso DB (local shard files, hosted vector stores) is inventoried by name and given a leg (restic file backup into the mesh repos) or an exclusion with reason.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Inventory posted on this issue: every embed
title: impl(backups): mesh coverage — embedding/shard stores restore without a re-embed pass

## Summary

The notes list a wish-list of further environments (alpine-slim, `FROM scratch`, distroless, flatpak, fedora-kde, silverblue/kinoite, ubuntu, windows-11) and justify it with "basically everything should work because static binary". This issue checks that claim. mcpx itself **can** be a static binary; what stands in the way is elsewhere:
1. **The shipped artifacts are not static -- by choice, not by necessity.** The default nix package is built with the nixpkgs cgo default and installed behind a C wrapper with nix-store paths baked in; #182's `Containerfile` keeps `ARG CGO_ENABLED=1` deliberately. A `CGO_ENABLED=0` build is fully static and works (verified in #182, `docs/container.md` §4). Which artifacts *should* be static is a policy decision (decision 1 below), not a feasibility question.
2. **`exec` needs a JS runtime**, which no minimal image has -- and bun, deno and git are dynamically linked distribution binaries, so a static `mcpx` beside them does not make an image static.
3. **mcpx does not compile for Windows today.**

It then assigns each environment a tier, says what it needs (a copied binary or an installer, and any extra config), and says which runner provides it.

## Original notes

> - testing
>

**Cache: deferred to #187** (#181 collision 12). #187 owns the cache mechanism
(layout, keys, eviction, leases); this issue owns what it puts in it — the
resolved import graph and the prepared environment. The cache text in stages 1
and 3 below stays as input to #187.

## Summary

When a script imports something that is not present, mcpx should be able to
work out what it needs and make it available — without an LLM in the loop, and
without executing the script. The static import graph of an ES module program
is fully determinable; the exceptions are enumerable and small. This issue
covers computing that graph, deciding what to do with the unresolved edges, and
the cross-directory case where an imported file belongs to a different project
with its own manifest and lockfile.

>   - if i import a file in another dir that has its own package.json/lock can it auto-import, prepare dependencies to be available whereever needed

## Summary

Today a script that calls a tool wrongly fails at the wrong moment: the error arrives from a server, halfway through, after the side effects of every call before it. `--diagnose-preflight` (#41) fixed the statically-detectable half. This issue is the rest of it — a graded ladder of what mcpx does when a request is *probably* wrong, from "refuse it deterministically" through "ask the caller" to "rewrite it and run the rewrite", with the escalation policy as a setting rather than a hard-coded behaviour.

The unifying idea: **an execution outcome should be a structured verdict, not a boolean.** "It failed" loses the fact that eleven of twelve calls succeeded, which of them had side effects, what specifically was wrong with the twelfth, and what the minimal fix is. mcpx already computes most of those facts and throws them away.

## Original notes

> - mcp-owned opencode api support
>   - receive errors check io and elicit/prompt caller, or fix-retry, clean up return what worked with explanation of what happened, pass-through
>   - check inputs, reject any request with/without reason, prompt 'hey are you sure? you did this and that maybe doesnt do what you think', 'hey i mean this probably cant work because y', or
title: mcpx: checking, refusing and repairing a request — a graded ladder from deterministic diagnostics to rewrite-and-run

The server VM booted cleanly (DHCP lease 10.0.2.15, multi-user target reached at ~47s) and then nothing satisfied the test before its timeout (~929s of kernel time in the final log).

## The gap

The 2026-11-13→16 Mistral outage (57h dark) had two halves. The first half is now closed: the CDP Helium browser carrying the Mistral console session died at a laptop reboot and nothing owned it. As of 2026-11-16 it runs under a supervised systemd user unit (`helium-cdp.service`, restart-on-failure, correct profile, kill/restart recovery proven live — see #6032 comment 6910076337).

The second half is still unbuilt, and it is the half that made the outage silent for 57 hours:

1. **No stale-read detection that leads anywhere.** When a console-scraped pool's read goes stale, the quota-check stale-source escalation exists on paper (it fired once, 2026-11-14, quota-check v71) but dedupe held it forever and no repair was ever dispatched. Detection must end in a repair action, not a note.

## From the #2059 investigation (hot-world sharding)

The landed investigation doc for #2059 (`doc/2026-10-30T19-35-00Z_investigation_hot_world_sharding/`, §3 rung 3) designs native-node spill for an indivisible hot world: a native `id` node runs the world's program turns while the hosted Durable Object keeps the journal of record. The doc is explicit that **the journaled single-writer lease is the whole safety design** — split-brain (DO and native node both accepting writes) is the catastrophic failure. The lease protocol itself was not designed. This issue designs it, so the #2046 synthesis adopts a designed protocol instead of a placeholder.

## Design to produce

- **Lease object**: grant/revoke/handoff as journaled entries — who grants (DO? coordinator? operator?), lease term and renewal, and how the grant is recorded so both sides and any auditor can prove who held the write lease at any journal position.
- **Fencing**: how a partitioned or crashed ex-holder is fenced out (monotonic lease epoch checked on journal append is the obvious shape — verify or replace), and what happens to writes an ex-holder attempts after losing the lease.
- **Handoff both ways**: DO → native at spill start, native → DO at de-escalation (investigation §2: spill ends when the warning band clears for ~1 hour), including in-flight command treatment at the boundary.
- **Failure walkthroughs**: native node crashes holding the lease; DO and node partitioned while both alive; lease expires mid-turn;
title: id: design: native-spill write lease protocol for hot worlds (from #2059)

# design: versioning for a monorepo whose apps deploy individually

**WS-H** · Design task (survey + interim policy), filed 2026-11-04. Related: epic #5765 (deployment architecture — services layer + deploy tool), #5766 (deploy tool v1), #5760 (fleet Nix-build state; the deployed-lag table that motivates this), PR #5764 (the services-layer design).

## Why

Under the NixOS system closure, "what version is running" was declarative: the system profile *was* the answer. The services-layer design (#5764) deliberately takes apps out of that closure so they can deploy individually — which buys deploy/rollback flexibility and sells the free identity answer. #5760 shows the failure mode already, before any of that lands: the deployed fleet binaries lag `pkgs/fleet` HEAD by five commits — including a proxy request-line validation hardening — and nothing noticed, because every one of those commits self-reports the same version string, `0.1.0`. A hand-maintained version constant does not move when code moves.

Drew's counter-measures (2026-11-04): every binary **self-reports** an embedded version (number + git hash) via `--version`/`--about` or its version verb; versions are **derived automatically** from tags + branch state so no two builds ever collide; monorepo releases use **per-app prefixed tags** for what was actually tested and shipped, **plus a whole-repo tag** for the commit; the numbers are **technically semver, loosely followed** — the constraint that matters is Rust consumer
title: design: versioning for a monorepo whose apps deploy individually — derived versions, per-app tags + repo date tag, survey of schemes (WS-H)

## Summary

`mcpx exec` runs a script and returns what it produced. This asks for the caller to be able to attach natural-language instructions to the *edges* of that run — before it, after it, on failure, on success — so the deterministic script stays deterministic and the fuzzy parts sit outside it.

That is a better factoring than it first appears. The script is the part that must be reproducible; "make sure these dependencies exist wherever this runs" and "clean up the results and transform them" are the parts that legitimately vary by environment and by caller. Keeping them out of the script means the same script file works everywhere and the variation is in the *options*, which is exactly the shape `ExecOptions` was designed for (#40, step 7: "not a new method, an option").

> - mcp-owned opencode api support
>   - accept prompt/prePrompt/postPrompt/onErrorPrompt/onSuccessPrompt
>     - the script interface just runs the scripts, but you can provide a prePrompt saying hey i added a bunch of dependencies please make sure they exist where the job runs, postPrompt to clean up the results and transform, either prompt/pre/post could say to fix error thing but onError gets provided above or below the er

Execution issue for tracked goal **CPU/memory load over time + parallelism efficiency** (goal_8c75ed164542). Filed 2026-11-07 on Drew's ruling that the census "dead" goals were dormant because the fleet never ran work against them.

## Question

What concurrency level makes the sandbox VM (and the laptop executors) finish the most work per credit? Drew's framing: CPU near 99% because it's performing at peak is the target — 95% while 35 things complete beats 8-vs-6 things grinding the whole box to a halt. Find the concurrency sweet spot **empirically**, then fold the answer into delegation/orchestration practice.

## Plan

- [ ] Baseline: load profile snapshot (done — first comment on this issue, 2026-11-07 18:49 CST)
- [ ] Sampled profile over time: load average, run-queue depth, CPU user/sys/idle/iowait/steal, memory + swap pressure, sampled across busy and quiet windows (not just one evening snapshot)
- [ ] Concurrency sweep: run controlled parallel work at several lane/agent concurrency levels and measure completed-work throughput + latency degradation per level
- [ ] Identify the noisy-neighbor cliff: the level where context-switch / iowait / steal growth eats the gains
- [ ] Write the delegation battle plan: who orchestrates, how work is tracked, concurrency defaults per machine, coordination-chatter budget
- [ ] Fold the defaults into the orchestration / lane runbooks so the finding changes behavior, not just this issue

## Acceptance

- [ ] A measured sweet-spot number
title: investigate: CPU/memory load over time + parallelism sweet spot on the sandbox VM
